content: 1. Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) vs. Conventional Care for Preterm Newborns Evidence from a Cochrane review (Conde-Agudelo et al., 2011) suggests that Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) may reduce morbidity and mortality in low birthweight infants. The quality of evidence is high, with an estimated reduction of 50 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 22 to 66 fewer). This intervention is considered critical for improving preterm birth outcomes. 2. Continuous Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) vs. Conventional Care Continuous KMC, compared to conventional care, showed a reduction of 40 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 5 to 59 fewer). The quality of evidence is moderate, and the intervention is deemed critical. However, the data is based on a single trial, limiting the ability to assess consistency. 3. Intermittent Kangaroo Mother Care (KMC) vs. Conventional Care Intermittent KMC demonstrated a reduction of 61 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 15 more to 119 fewer). The quality of evidence is moderate, and the intervention is critical. Wide confidence intervals and a small number of events limit the precision of the findings. 4. Radiant Warmers vs. Incubators for Unstable or Sick Preterm Newborns Radiant warmers, compared to incubators, showed very low-quality evidence with an increase of 21 more deaths per 1,000 live births. The evidence is considered important but is limited by design flaws, lack of blinding, and the inclusion of studies from high-income countries only. 5. Plastic Bags or Wraps vs. Conventional Care Immediately After Birth The use of plastic bags or wraps for preterm newborns immediately after birth showed a reduction of 151 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 209 fewer to 345 more). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income settings, with wide confidence intervals and some heterogeneity. 6. Continuous Positive Airway Pressure (CPAP) Therapy for Respiratory Distress Syndrome (RDS) CPAP therapy for preterm newborns with RDS showed an increase of 87 more deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 16 to 224 more). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. Limitations include unclear allocation concealment, lack of blinding, and studies conducted in high-income countries. 7. Early vs. Late Initiation of CPAP Therapy for RDS Early initiation of CPAP therapy compared to late initiation showed a reduction of 24 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 93 fewer to 135 more). The quality of evidence is very low, and the intervention is critical. The findings are limited by unclear allocation concealment and wide confidence intervals. 8. Surfactant Replacement Therapy with Animal-Derived Surfactants for RDS Animal-derived surfactant therapy showed a reduction of 18 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 59 fewer to 30 more). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with significant heterogeneity and wide confidence intervals. 9. Surfactant Replacement Therapy with Protein-Free Synthetic Surfactants for RDS Protein-free synthetic surfactants showed a reduction of 13 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 1 fewer to 1 fewer). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. 10. Protein-Free Synthetic Surfactants vs. Natural Surfactants for RDS Protein-free synthetic surfactants compared to natural surfactants showed a reduction of 7 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 23 fewer to 12 more). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with subjective outcomes and lack of blinding. 11. Protein-Containing Synthetic Surfactants vs. Natural Surfactants for RDS Protein-containing synthetic surfactants compared to natural surfactants showed a reduction of 55 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 19 fewer to 80 fewer). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with significant heterogeneity. 12. Prophylactic vs. Rescue Surfactant Therapy with or without CPAP for RDS Prophylactic surfactant therapy compared to rescue therapy showed a reduction of 16 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 34 fewer to 7 more). The quality of evidence is very low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with wide confidence intervals crossing the line of no effect. 13. Prophylactic vs. Rescue Surfactant Therapy without CPAP for RDS Prophylactic surfactant therapy without CPAP showed a reduction of 31 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 8 fewer to 47 fewer). The quality of evidence is low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with wide confidence intervals and lack of blinding. 14. Prophylactic vs. Rescue Surfactant Therapy with CPAP for RDS Prophylactic surfactant therapy with CPAP showed a reduction of 18 fewer deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 24 more to 50 fewer). The quality of evidence is very low, and the intervention is critical. The studies were conducted in high-income countries, with wide confidence intervals and lack of blinding. 15. Early vs. Late Surfactant Therapy for RDS Early surfactant therapy (within 2–3 hours of birth) compared to late therapy (after symptoms worsen) showed an increase of 54 more deaths per 1,000 live births (ranging from 3 fewer to 157 more). The quality of evidence is very low, and the intervention is critical. The findings are limited by lack of blinding, absence of trials from lowand middle-income countries, and wide confidence intervals. These findings highlight the variability in evidence quality and the critical importance of interventions to improve outcomes for preterm newborns.
